english_verification.review_scope: Representative current-Mod checks for opening identity, the captain revolt, and same-Tag rename; read the relevant fixed-revision Wiki chunk for the Mureda Accord, captaincy, and Raheni-colonisation context. The 31-mission count and remaining narrative details follow the supplied evidence; no exhaustive mission audit was performed. The primary compared native idea names/descriptions with current English localisation keys (formatting codes stripped); original sources and optional sets are kept separate. Wide source bounds are locator envelopes, not exhaustive line-by-line audits. No formal validators, tests, builds or browser checks were run.
unresolved: The Wiki is setting history and does not determine current mission mechanics or guarantee later outcomes.
The supplied prior evidence reports no dedicated L55 Tag-changing formable, but does not exhaustively traverse generic formable decisions.
Player reports are version-limited and difficulty was not measured in-game.

rationale.campaign_length: The structured index identifies 31 direct L55 missions; the second part appears by country flag and is not a separate Tag’s tree.
rationale.colonization: Southern islands and the Insyaa objective involve colonisation, but do not replace the naval-conquest core loop.
rationale.complexity: Authority variables, internal revolt, a mission-tree transition, maritime supply, land warfare, and trade goals must be managed together.
rationale.dark_story: Raiding, coercive rule, and forced-spouse events are dark aspects; urban order and public works make the story less one-sided.
rationale.difficulty: Naval superiority does not solve a weak land economy, colonial powers, or mutiny pressure; difficulty has not been measured in-game.
rationale.diplomacy: The domestic struggle between the matriarch and captains is prominent, while pirate reputation constrains foreign diplomacy.
rationale.early_pressure: The opening narrative says colonists are closing in and the internal alliance is fracturing; player reports also describe weak finances and few allies.
rationale.magic_artifice_intensity: Siren song and the Sky-domain religion have supernatural aspects, but the country centres on naval politics rather than a mage institution.
rationale.narrative_density: The Muréda Accord, captains’ conclave, mutiny, Ríva’s reforms, and gulf-empire ambitions make a coherent arc.
rationale.tall_play: Songhouses, ports, and development of Yetmesira matter, but the overall tree favours maritime expansion.
rationale.trade_economy: Raiding, privateering ports, gulf trade routes, and Raheni trade income form the fiscal core.
rationale.warfare: Coastal conquest, anti-colonial wars, overseas landings, and marines run throughout the missions.

identity.appearance: An established harpy pirate republic in 1444; it later changes to a monarchy after a mutiny and is renamed Ríva Naléni under the same Tag.
identity.formation_scope: No dedicated Tag-changing formable has been established; the Captains’ Conclave triggers a government and mission transition, while the a_new_naleni mission only changes the name and raises rank, retaining L55.

national_ideas.scope_note: National traditions, seven national ideas and ambition only; optional idea groups and racial/government bonuses are excluded. Conditional alternatives are separate, not stacked. Accepting new ideas on formation depends on the actual event/decision and player choice.

description.text: The Pirate-Harpies of Naléni were once disorganized flocks, but as they grew stronger and consolidated, they began to spread out beyond the reaches of Telekenid. The sharp wit and quick tongues of their leaders let them strike deals and cut across courts, stitching together a small pirate empire out of the husk of the old Irkan Eparta before anyone could begin to realize how much land was held under their wings and sails.

description.text: Harpies spend their entire lives hunting, and the Pirates of Naléni are no different. They have a fine eye for quality in what they want, both men and treasure. This allows for quick and effective decisions to be made when they raid coastal towns, cities or rival shipping vessels, as to which men would work best under the decks of the galley as rowing slaves, or above board as the soldiers of their newfound 'masters'.

description.text: Sailors hear tales of the Siren, their songs deadly lures for those without their wits about them. Many believe these to be fantasy - tales to scare children at night, and excuses by husbands caught in scandalous affairs. The Harpies of Naléni, however, bring reality to these tales, our songs having lured many an unsuspecting enemy into lowering their guard at a vital moment in combat.

description.text: The Harpies of Naléni have built a league of trading factors throughout the Isles of the Ringlet Sea. They serve double purpose; as both merchants and as strong-arms, negotiating 'protection fees' to do business in the local ports, as well as reminders of how cheap the price of their protection is. An exchange of coin is far less costly than a return visit from a Nalénian ship, after all.

description.text: In an attempt to strengthen relationships with the Busilari court, Nalénians converted to the Ravelian Church in wake of their increased influence in the Ringlet Isles. The Church would later use the Nalénian cities as a center of operations across East Sarhal. A positive effect of this was the development of centers of Artifice research and education systems - funded by either the Church itself or particularly wealthy Rectors with an interest in the region.

description.text: Piracy has existed in Sarhal for aeons, but few are as skilled at it as the Nalénian Harpies. Able to utilize their wings, they can raid further from home and keep their ships further ashore, safe from potential defenses. This has been perfected over generations to allow expeditions farther and farther afield, bringing winged raids to new shores, rich with new men and new treasure.

description.text: Naléni has carried forth a tradition of the former kingdom of Irkan Eparta; the display of authority and rule by carving the heads of their leaders into the sides of the Emot Nepas Sedar. The Harpies construct their additions higher than that of the humans - whether or not this is a show of superiority over their subjects is a matter of debate within Naléni. Naléni’s inherently factional political structure has led to each ruler feeling pressure to outdo their predecessor, leading to demands for more and more statues carved into the mountainside upon ruler succession. While expensive, this has concentrated a wealth of stoneworking and construction expertise into our realm.

player_overview.avoid_if: Avoid if you only want peaceful development or land warfare, do not want to manage naval power and rebels, or dislike raiding and coercive rule as themes.
player_overview.how_it_plays: Use the navy, raiding, and coastal warfare to survive the opening; experience the captains’ mutiny and transition to monarchy in the middle; then expand across the sea into Rahen, develop Menji lands, and contest gulf trade.
player_overview.overview: Begin as Naléni on the Great Horn at the edge of the Gulf of Rahen, with a fleet but a fragile accord between the matriarch and independent pirate captains. Capturing ports, raiding, and training sirens can help repel colonists, but the Captains’ Conclave ignites a mutiny and ushers in Queen Ríva’s second mission arc. You then turn pirates into controlled privateers and use songhouses, ports, and marines to rule both shores. The new country name remains under L55; it is not a different formable Tag.
player_overview.recommended_for: Players who enjoy pirates, marines, port economies, internal coups, and a two-part national story.
signature_features: Matriarchal authority changes through events and affects post-mutiny legitimacy and rebel pressure.
Sirens are both elite combatants and central to Menji songhouses and social control.
Two mission phases under the same Tag develop a raiding port into a cross-sea trade, privateering, and naval power.
player_overview.tagline: Lead harpy pirates through their internal feud and turn the Great Horn into your maritime empire.

reasons: The power struggle between pirates and the matriarch drives the first act.
Sirens and marines give the fleet a distinctive identity.
A same-Tag transition after the mutiny connects raiding to privateering, trade, and rule in the second act.
warnings: The early economy and land warfare can be difficult.
The Captains’ Conclave is followed by a revolt that must be suppressed.
The missions involve raiding and coercive rule over subjects.

positive_indicators: Invests in Yetmesira’s city and trade infrastructure.
The later state attempts to protect merchant ships that pay for protection.
Some events recognise the ability of individual Menji women to command ships.
values.rationale: Resistance to Raheni colonisation, warfare, monarchy, and overseas expansion are not penalised in themselves. Urban investment, songhouses, protection for paying merchants, and recognition of some Menji women’s command ability provide limited public benefit and personhood. However, maritime raiding, intimidation and instrumentalisation of human subjects, and coercion in spouse-arrangement events reduce dignity and restraint. Refurbishing former slave ports does not prove abolition; later routes are safer only on conditions of payment and compliance. The country combines protection with predation, so it is provisionally Neutral rather than Good.
red_flags: Pirate raiding and privateering ports remain part of the national loop.
Songhouses and sirens also serve purposes of social control.
Some events forcibly assign Menji men as spouses.
